definition: Pariah means an outcast; a person shunned by those around them.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word pariah. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know pariah should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: In the novel's third act, the debt collector realizes he has become the island's pariah: shutters latch as he walks the lane, and even the ferryman will not meet his eye.
An outsider is a far milder case than a pariah: an outsider simply is not part of the group yet — the door is closed but nobody guards it — while a pariah is actively driven off at every turn.
Outcast is milder than pariah: an outcast has been pushed out of one circle, while a pariah is shunned by practically everyone, everywhere they turn.

An exile has been forced out of a place and must physically stay away — the distance is geographic. A pariah can stay exactly where they are and still be utterly alone, because it is the people, not the place, that have shut them out.

A misfit simply does not fit in — awkward, out of step, in the wrong crowd — but nobody is organizing against them. A pariah is made, not born: the group shuns them deliberately, door by door, and keeps on doing it.
someone accepted at the group's center
the one the group prizes most

Because pariah arrived whole from Tamil — one of the few everyday English words that did — it shares no root with anything else you will read. There is no 'pari-' family to spot; the word stands alone, and its drumbeat origin survives only in dictionaries.
Pariah means an outcast; a person shunned by those around them.
The critic who panned the town's beloved festival returned the next year a pariah — hoteliers 'lost' his booking, and the shuttle to the fairground was somehow always full.
Pariah is stronger than outsider or misfit because it names someone actively shunned by nearly everyone around them — not merely unknown or awkward, but avoided on purpose, door by door.
Pariah is a strong, headline-ready word: states, executives, and neighbors can all be pariahs, but only when the shunning is near-total.
For milder cases reach for outcast or outsider.
Ostracism, taught in this unit, names the treatment; the pariah is the person it lands on.
The word began as a caste name, so it always carries a shadow of unearned exclusion.

In 1847 the Viennese obstetrician Ignaz Semmelweis ordered his students to wash their hands in chlorinated lime before entering the maternity ward, and deaths on his ward fell almost at once.
The reward for being right was swift.
Colleagues bristled at the suggestion that their own hands carried death from the autopsy room to new mothers.
Within a few years Semmelweis had become a pariah in Viennese medicine: journals mocked his data, hospitals declined to renew his post, and former allies stopped answering his letters.
He had not been banished from the city — he could walk into any lecture hall in Vienna.
What had closed was every door held by a colleague.
Not until decades after his death, when germ theory triumphed, did the profession admit that the man it had frozen out had been right all along.
